objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain night vision, airport and airplane lighting, night navigation, illusions, taxi and traffic recognition at commercial-pilot depth, and you can plan, brief, fly and debrief a learner's first night lesson that meets the 14 CFR 61.109 and 61.87(o) training rules.
why: Night changes nothing about how the airplane flies, but it changes a great deal about what the pilot can see and judge [[24:218|AFH 11-1]]. The night VFR accident rate drops by nearly half once a pilot reaches 100 hours, so the night hours you give a learner come at the riskiest point of their flying life [[25:13|AIH 1-9]]. The CFI checkride asks you to teach at least one of the night knowledge elements, and every private learner you train needs your night training unless an exception applies [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(2)]].

prereading.what: The whole night operations chapter: vision, illusions, equipment, lighting, training for night flight, takeoff, landing and night emergencies.
prereading.label: AFH 11-1 to 11-14

prereading.what: Rods and cones, vision types, night blind spot, dark adaptation, scanning, night vision protection and night illusions.
prereading.label: PHAK 17-20 to 17-27

prereading.what: Visual illusions, spatial disorientation demonstrations and how to cope with them.
prereading.label: PHAK 17-8 to 17-10

prereading.what: Visual glide path lights, runway and taxiway lights, runway entrance lights, pilot-controlled lighting, beacons and obstruction lights.
prereading.label: AIM 2-1-2 to 2-2-3

prereading.what: Illusions on landing, vision in flight, dark adaptation, scanning and judging a collision course.
prereading.label: AIM 8-1-5 to 8-1-8

prereading.what: Night currency, student night solo, and the night training you must give for private and commercial certificates.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.57, 61.87, 61.109, 61.129

prereading.what: Demonstration-performance, telling-and-doing, primacy and the positive exchange of flight controls.
prereading.label: AIH 9-5 to 9-9

warmup: Think first: your private learner has 32 hours, has never flown after dark, and the schedule gives you one evening this week. What would you teach on the ground before engine start, what would you show first in the air, and what one thing would make you cancel the flight at the airplane?

key_terms.def: Night vision under low light, when the cones are ineffective; acuity falls to 20/200 or less and color is lost [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]].
Dawn, dusk or full-moon vision using both rods and cones. The PHAK calls it the most dangerous period for viewing [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]].
The center 5 to 10 degrees of the visual field, which goes blind in low light because the fovea has no rods [[24:220|AFH 11-3]].
The eye growing more sensitive in darkness. Up to 30 minutes for full adaptation [[24:220|AFH 11-3]]; a moderate degree in about 20 minutes under dim red cockpit light [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]].
Looking about 10 degrees above, below or to either side of an object so the rods can see it [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].
A still light that seems to move after you stare at it; movement starts in about 8 to 10 seconds [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]].
A landing from over water or unlit land where the runway lights are the only light; the worst case is landing short [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].
Airport lights turned on by keying the microphone 7, 5 or 3 times within 5 seconds on a set frequency [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].
Precision approach path indicator: a row of two or four light units that show white above and red below the glide path, visible up to 20 miles at night [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]].
Red in-pavement lights at a taxiway that warn the runway is unsafe to enter; they never replace an ATC clearance [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6]].
Practicing maneuvers with all flight deck lights OFF to simulate an electrical or instrument light failure [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].
The three-step 'You have the flight controls' / 'I have the flight controls' / 'You have the flight controls' handover [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

chunks.title: The night training you must give

body.p: As a CFI you are the person who supplies the night training the regulations require. Know each rule cold, because a learner who is short one landing is short of the certificate.

head: Who
Night training or experience
Rule
rows: 3 hours of night flight training that includes one cross-country of over 100 NM total distance and 10 takeoffs and 10 landings to a full stop, each with a flight in the traffic pattern
Training from an authorized instructor [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(2)]]
Night training at the solo airport on takeoffs, approaches, landings and go-arounds; night navigation training near that airport; a make and model night solo endorsement
Instructor who gave the training within the 90 days before the flight [[60:277|14 CFR 61.87(o)]]
One 2-hour night cross-country of more than 100 NM straight-line distance with an instructor, and 5 hours of night VFR with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings at an airport with an operating control tower
Training and solo or PIC time [[60:315|14 CFR 61.129(a)(3)(iv)]] [[60:315|14 CFR 61.129(a)(4)(ii)]]
3 takeoffs and 3 full-stop landings in the preceding 90 days, made between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise

body.p: Night for logging and for 91.205(c) is the 14 CFR 1.1 night, from the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]. Plan the 61.109 lesson so the time you log falls inside that window.

bullets: The A.5 endorsement certifies night training at the named solo airport and nearby night navigation; it expires 90 calendar days from the date of the night training [[12:41|AC 61-65K A.5]].
A student seeking a sport pilot certificate may not act as PIC at night at all [[12:15|AC 61-65K 20.4]].

A learner who trains in and lives in Alaska may skip the night training and receive a certificate marked 'Night flying prohibited'; the training must then be done within 12 calendar months or the certificate becomes invalid for use [[60:306|14 CFR 61.110]] [[60:307|14 CFR 61.110(b)(2)]].
A commercial pilot without an instrument rating gets a limitation prohibiting carriage of passengers for hire on cross-countries over 50 NM or at night [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(b)(1)]].

callout.text: Private: 3, 100, 10 (hours, NM total, full-stop landings). Commercial: 2 hours and 100 NM straight line dual, then 5 hours and 10 landings at a towered field.

Meeting the hours is not the goal. The AFH says learning to fly safely at night takes time and experience, and lists the maneuvers to practice at night, from straight-and-level flight to steep turns [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].

check.q: Your private learner logged 3.2 hours of night training with a 104 NM total distance cross-country and 7 full-stop landings plus 3 touch-and-goes. Is 61.109(a)(2) met?
check.a: No. It needs 10 takeoffs and 10 landings to a full stop [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(2)(ii)]].

chunks.title: K1: The eye at night, taught so it sticks

body.p: Start the ground lesson with the eye, because every later night technique comes from it.

bullets: Cones sit mostly in the center of the retina; the fovea holds cones only. They give detail, color and far-away identification in good light [[24:218|AFH 11-1]].
Rods sit mainly in the periphery, which is about 10,000 times more sensitive to light than the fovea. They see in shades of gray, with no detail or color [[24:218|AFH 11-1]].
In the absence of normal light, night vision falls almost entirely on the rods [[24:219|AFH 11-2]].

head: Vision type
Light
What the learner should expect
rows: Central foveal vision gives sharp images and color [[24:219|AFH 11-2]]
Acuity and color fade; the most dangerous period for viewing, so use off-center vision and scanning [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]]
Acuity 20/200 or less: at 20 feet you see what you would see at 200 feet by day [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]]

body.p: The night blind spot covers the central 5 to 10 degrees of the field. An object viewed directly may go unseen, or fade after first being seen, and the blind spot can hide larger objects as distance increases [[24:220|AFH 11-3]]. Depth perception and size judgment may also be lost at night [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].

Do not confuse it with the central blind spot at the optic disk, which every eye has day and night. Binocular vision covers it unless one eye's view is blocked, for example by a windshield divider [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]].

callout.text: Teach it by doing it. PHAK Figure 17-15 is a page test that makes an X vanish in the optic disk blind spot [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]]. Outside on a full-moon night, have the learner cover the left eye and slide the right eye left until only the halo of the moon remains [[1:444|PHAK 17-22]]. A learner who has watched an object disappear believes the off-center rule.
Monovision contact lenses suppress one eye at a time and impair depth perception; the FAA recommends not using them when piloting [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]. Ask about them in the briefing.

check.q: Why does a learner lose a dim light ahead when looking straight at it?
check.a: The fovea has no rods, so the center 5 to 10 degrees of the field is blind in low light [[24:220|AFH 11-3]].

chunks.title: K1, K5 and R5: Managing dark adaptation in the cockpit

body.p: Dark adaptation is slow to build and quick to lose. The rods can take about 30 minutes to fully adapt, and a bright light can wipe out the adaptation so the process must start over [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]]. Moving from a bright room into the dark takes longer than moving from a dim room [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].

head: Phase of the lesson
What protects night vision
rows: N-15 neutral density sunglasses in bright sun speed dark adaptation that night [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]]; prolonged bright sun impairs it [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]]
Brief in a dim room (application of the bright-room fact above); white light for the walkaround, red for flight deck work [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]
Dim the flight deck lights to the minimum that lets you read instruments and switches; this also kills windshield reflections [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]
Allow time to adjust: readjust instrument lights and reorient to outside references; night vision keeps improving [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]]
Close one eye when bright exposure begins [[24:220|AFH 11-3]]; turn away and fly the edge of a brightly lit area [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]]

body.p: Red light preserves outside vision, but it severely distorts colors on charts and can make it hard to focus on things inside; use it only where the best outside night vision is needed, and keep white light available for map and instrument reading [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]]. Under red light magenta and yellow look red and cyan looks black [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]. A moderate degree of adaptation comes in 20 minutes under dim red light; complete adaptation needs at least 30 minutes of total darkness [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]].

Scanning at night depends almost entirely on peripheral vision [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]]. Teach the PHAK pattern: scan right to left or left to right, starting far and working in, about 30 degrees per stop, no stop longer than 2 to 3 seconds, overlapping the last field by 10 degrees [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].

head: Things that steal night vision
Effect
rows: Night vision declines measurably above 4,000 ft pressure altitude; after 30 minutes at 12,000 ft, acuity may not return for over an hour after descending [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]]
The worst self-imposed stressor for night sensitivity; a 20 percent loss at sea level, like a physiological altitude of 5,000 ft [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]]
Pilots stare and stop scanning; exhausted pilots fixate on instruments [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]]
Low blood sugar shortens attention; lack of vitamin A impairs night vision, though extra does not improve it [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]]

callout.text: Any degree of dark adaptation is lost within a few seconds of viewing a bright light [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]]. The most common thief is a white flashlight swept across the cockpit; the PHAK says never shine it in your own or another crewmember's eyes [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]].

check.q: You need to read a chart with magenta airspace at night. Which light, and why?
check.a: Dim white. Red light makes magenta look red [[24:221|AFH 11-4]], and white light must be available for map reading [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]].

chunks.title: K2: Airport, runway, taxiway and obstruction lights

body.p: Airports away from cities stand out by their runway lights, but airports in or near cities blend into city lights; know where the airport sits relative to the city and its lighting pattern [[24:223|AFH 11-6]]. Before any night cross-country, check the destination's lighting on the chart, in the Chart Supplement and in NOTAMs [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].

head: Light
What it shows
Source
rows: 24 to 30 flashes per minute for an airport; white and green for a lighted land airport, two quick white flashes then green for a military airport
White; on instrument runways yellow on the last 2,000 ft or half the runway, whichever is less
Green toward landing airplanes, red toward departing ones
A pair of synchronized flashing lights at the threshold to find a runway among other lights or with poor contrast
Blue edge lights; steady green centerline lights
Alternating green and yellow while you are inside the runway environment or ILS critical area
Three steady yellow in-pavement lights at a taxiway holding position
Flashing yellow pair or in-pavement yellow row at the runway holding position
Red row across the taxiway; never cross it lit, even with a clearance
Flashing red beacons (20 to 40 per minute) and steady red at night; flashing high-intensity white on some towers and wire supports

body.p: Visual glide path lights. A 2-bar VASI gives one glide path normally set at 3 degrees and gives safe obstruction clearance within 10 degrees of the extended centerline out to 4 NM [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2]]. The PAPI is a single row of two or four units, usually on the left side, visible up to 20 miles at night, with obstruction clearance to 3.4 NM [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]].

callout.text: Do not start a descent on the VASI or PAPI until the airplane is visually aligned with the runway; lateral guidance comes from the runway lights [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]].

body.p: Pilot-controlled lighting: key the microphone 7, 5 or 3 times within 5 seconds for highest, medium or lowest intensity; the lights stay on 15 minutes from the last activation [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]]. Receivers may be set to low sensitivity because nearby airports share frequencies, so key again when overflying the airport or just before final [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]]. The frequency is in the Chart Supplement, not on the sectional [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

callout.text: Teaching tip: fly the learner over the airport at altitude before the first landing and have them call out each light group by color. AFH suggests an aerial look at unfamiliar airports before landing when possible [[24:230|AFH 11-13]].

check.q: Taxiing out, the learner sees alternating green and yellow centerline lights. Where is the airplane?
check.a: Inside the runway environment or ILS critical area; the lead-on and lead-off lights are color-coded to warn of it [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5]].

chunks.title: K3 and K4: The airplane, its lights, and the flight bag

body.p: For VFR at night, 91.205(c) adds to the day list: approved position lights; an approved red or white anticollision light system; one electric landing light if the airplane is operated for hire; an adequate source of electrical energy for all installed electrical and radio equipment; and one spare set of fuses or three of each kind, accessible in flight [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]].

bullets: Position lights must be lit from sunset to sunrise; an airplane equipped with anticollision lights must have them lit, but the PIC may turn them off when that is in the interest of safety [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]].
If any anticollision light fails, the flight may continue to a stop where it can be repaired [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(3)]].
Position lights are a red light on the left side, a green light on the right side spaced as far apart as practicable, and a white light facing aft [[60:118|14 CFR 23.2530(c)]].
The IFR instruments of 91.205(d) are valuable for aircraft control at night even on a VFR flight [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].
Night VFR fuel: enough to reach the first point of intended landing and fly 45 more minutes at normal cruise [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]].

body.p: Preflight the lights, not just the airplane: turn every light on briefly and tap the position light fixtures; if a light blinks when tapped, find the cause before flight [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

Personal equipment. At least one reliable flashlight is standard on every night flight, preferably a dimmable white and red light, big enough to find easily, with spare batteries [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]. White is for the walkaround, red for flight deck operations, dim white for charts; some pilots carry a second red penlight on a string around the neck [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]. Add charts (including the adjacent chart near an edge), flight data and a checklist covering before start, before takeoff, cruise, before landing, after landing, stopping engines and emergencies [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]. An EFB works if its brightness is turned down [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].

callout.text: Make the learner's flight bag part of the lesson. The AIH lists 'is a flashlight available that suits the flight' and 'were the lights found operational' among the special night questions [[25:10|AIH 1-6]]. Have the learner lay everything out and place it within reach before taxi [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].
A part 91 airplane flown not for hire needs no landing light, but an inoperative one still makes night operation more hazardous [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

check.q: Which 91.205(c) item applies only when the airplane is operated for hire?

chunks.title: K5: Night orientation, navigation and chart reading

body.p: Night cross-countries present no special problems when pre-planning is adequate; monitor position, time, fuel and NAVAIDs just as in daylight [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].

bullets: Draw course lines in black so they show in low light [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
Use rotating beacons, lighted obstructions, city and town lights and highway traffic as checkpoints [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
Carry the adjacent chart: town lights can be seen at surprising distances, and without the chart they cannot be identified [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].
Load all GPS waypoints before flight and check the database before takeoff and again in flight [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
Plan safe altitudes ahead of time from the maximum elevation figures and other chart data, especially at night [[25:10|AIH 1-6]].

head: Sectional symbol
Meaning for the night plan
rows: Runway lights on from dusk to dawn [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]]
Lighting limitations exist (on request, part-time or pilot-controlled); check the Chart Supplement [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]]
Star on top of the airport symbol
Rotating or flashing beacon from dusk to dawn [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]]

body.p: Finding the runway: fly toward the rotating beacon until the lights that outline the runway can be told apart; positively identify the threshold and edge lights before flying the pattern, then keep them in sight [[24:227|AFH 11-10]]. At 2,000 ft a group of lights may show separately; at 5,000 ft or higher they may merge into one mass [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

callout.text: The PHAK suggests flying the routes you will fly at night first in daylight and choosing the minimum altitude you will accept at night; if weather forces you below it, decide early to turn around [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]. Build your learner's first night cross-country on a route you flew together by day.

check.q: The sectional shows an asterisk with the airport lighting symbol. What does the learner do before a night arrival?
check.a: Check the Chart Supplement for the lighting limitation, such as part-time or pilot-controlled lighting [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]].

chunks.title: K6: Using the instruments to verify attitude

body.p: The biggest difference at night is how few outside references remain, so the instruments carry more of the load, especially on takeoff and climb [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

head: Phase
Instrument cross-check
Source
rows: Set or check the heading indicator to the runway; keep the airplane between and parallel to the edge lights
Attitude indicator, VSI and altimeter all show a positive climb, airspeed at best climb; pitch and bank from the attitude and heading indicators
Heading bug on runway heading as a reference for pattern legs; altimeter and airspeed carry more weight because distance is deceptive
Cross-check altimeter and VSI against position; use the VASI

body.p: Practice by building blocks: straight-and-level flight, climbs and descents, level turns, climbing and descending turns and steep turns at night. Unusual attitude recovery should be practiced only with a flight instructor. Fly these with the flight deck lights OFF as well as ON to simulate an electrical or instrument light failure [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].

callout.text: Do not fly into dusk or darkness unless proficient in the flight instruments; when a visible horizon is missing, as over open water at night, obtain training and stay proficient in instrument control first [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].

Spatial disorientation demonstrations are taught in Human Factors (AI.II.A). Never do them at low altitude or without an instructor or safety pilot [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]]. On a night lesson, a short attitude-instrument segment over a dark area shows the learner why the AFH says to rely on the instruments.

check.q: Right after a night lift-off, which three instruments should all agree on a positive climb?
check.a: Attitude indicator, vertical speed indicator and altimeter, with airspeed at best climb [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

chunks.title: K7 and R5: Night illusions in every phase, and how to show them

body.p: Darkness or low visibility increases the chance of error, and false horizon and autokinesis affect the visual system alone [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]. Teach each illusion with the phase of flight where it bites.

head: Illusion
Phase
What happens
Defense
rows: Ground lights and stars blend; geometric light patterns, a sloping cloud or an aurora give a wrong horizon [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]; shoreline lights look like stars [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]
A light stared at moves on its own after 8 to 10 seconds [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]
Scan; the most important cure; do not stare more than 10 seconds [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]
Flickering light causes nausea, dizziness or confusion [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]
Screen out the light source [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]; proper scanning [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]
Eyes relax to a 10 to 30 ft focus; looking without seeing
Search out and focus on distant lights, however dim [[1:444|PHAK 17-22]]
An airplane seems to move away while closing; a light changing brightness reads as moving [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]] [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]
Feel higher than you are and fly a lower approach [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]; worst case, land short [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]
VASI, glideslope or instruments; go around when in doubt [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]
Bright runway lights, few lights around
Runway seems closer; tendency to fly high [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]
Few lights on the way in; city on higher terrain beyond
Tendency to fly lower than normal [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]
Review the airfield layout before the approach [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]
Can make the airplane seem higher than when wings are level [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]
Students lock on the instruments or the landing and miss ground closure [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]
Point it out when it happens [[25:83|AIH 3-32]]

body.p: Rain on the windscreen creates an illusion of greater height, haze one of greater distance; both lead to a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

bullets: Prevention, AFH list: expect illusions at unfamiliar airports at night; read airport diagrams and the Chart Supplement for slope, terrain and lighting; check the altimeter often; use VASI, PAPI or an electronic glideslope; use a VDP where published; know distractions raise accident risk; stay proficient in landings [[24:230|AFH 11-13]].

callout.text: Teach the black hole on the ground with the approach plate or airport diagram, then fly a normal approach to a runway with a PAPI and ask the learner to say the PAPI colors aloud every few seconds. Anticipating an illusion and staying aware of it is usually the best way to avoid it [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]].

check.q: On a night approach over few lights toward a runway with a city on higher terrain beyond, which way will the learner err?
check.a: Low. Both cues tend to produce a lower than normal approach [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].

chunks.title: K8 and R6: Night taxi and runway incursions

body.p: Check the parking ramp with a flashlight before getting in: ladders, holes and chocks that are obvious by day are hard to see at night [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]. Clear the propeller area with extra care; the beacon or a flash of the position lights warns people, but scan the area methodically [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

bullets: Taxi or landing light on to taxi, but watch electrical load and light overheating, and do not blind other pilots [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
Taxi slowly, follow the painted lines, and check instruments while taxiing [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
The taxi diagram, signs, markings and instruments should all agree; if anything conflicts, do not continue the taxi or the takeoff [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
Hold or lock the brakes during the run-up; forward creep is hard to see at night [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

head: Exterior lights
When
Source
rows: Before taxi; strobes off if they affect other pilots or ground crew
On when moving or about to move; off when stopped or yielding
Taxiing on or across any runway, at the PIC's discretion
Entering the runway to take off or line up and wait

body.p: Runway incursion defenses at night:

bullets: Low visibility raises incursion risk; do all heads-down tasks while stopped [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(4)]].

Unsure of your location: do not stop on a runway; stop, tell ATC, and ask for progressive taxi if needed. Runway centerlines are white and segmented, taxiway centerlines continuous yellow [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]].

Cleared to line up and wait at night: consider lining up about 3 ft left or right of centerline so a landing pilot can tell you from the runway lights [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(e)]]. If you were not told why you are waiting and hear nothing from ATC within 90 seconds, call them [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(9)]].
Red Runway Entrance Lights mean stop at the hold line or stay stopped, and call ATC if the clearance conflicts [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6]].

Expectation bias often happens while taxiing: pilots hear the route they expected, not the one given [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. The NTSB has found it in many night VMC events, where fewer cues help identify airports and runways [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

callout.text: A wrong turn, a wrong-surface takeoff or a takeoff on a closed runway can be catastrophic; preventing them depends on keeping situational awareness while moving on the ground [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

check.q: Your learner becomes unsure of position at a dark intersection near a runway. What do you have them do?
check.a: Stop (not on a runway), advise ATC and request progressive taxi if needed [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]].

chunks.title: K9 and R3: Reading traffic by its lights, and collision hazards

body.p: With only position lights to go on, the learner must work out direction of travel from color and position. The arrangement is the same as a boat's: red on the left wingtip, green on the right, white on the tail [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].

head: You see
Interpretation
Source
rows: Red on the left, green on the right
Flying the same direction as you; keep clear
Green on the left, red on the right
Could be on a collision course (coming toward you)
You are looking at its tail, since the white light faces aft
Lights growing brighter, no lateral or vertical motion
Closing on a collision course; take evasive action
Lights above or below the horizon
Probably higher or lower than you

body.p: Application of the right-of-way rule: when aircraft of the same category converge at about the same altitude (except head-on, or nearly so), the one to the other's right has the right-of-way [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]. So a lone red light ahead of your right wingtip, at about your altitude, that holds its place in the windshield and grows brighter is the left side of an airplane converging from your right: it has the right-of-way, so you give way (application). A light that drifts across the windshield or dims is not on a collision course.

bullets: Aircraft lights can blend with stars or city lights unless the learner makes a conscious effort to separate them [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].
Conflicting ground lights make other aircraft harder to detect; scan the area around a dim light rather than the light itself [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]].
Landing lights on below 10,000 ft, day or night, especially within 10 miles of an airport, help others see you; but not all aircraft have lights or use them [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].
Collision hazards rise where aircraft cluster: airways near VORs and Class B, C, D and E surface areas [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

callout.text: A red and green pair with red on the right: coming toward you. Red on the left: going your way. White alone: its tail. Brighter and still: collision course.

check.q: Ahead you see only a white light that slowly grows brighter. What is happening?
check.a: You are behind the other airplane (the white light faces aft) and closing on it [[60:118|14 CFR 23.2530(c)]] [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]].

chunks.title: R1 and R2: Inoperative equipment and weather you cannot see

body.p: Inoperative equipment. Without an MEL, an item may be inoperative for takeoff only if it is not required by the VFR-day type certificate, the equipment list or kinds of operations list, 91.205 for the kind of flight, or an AD; it is removed or deactivated and placarded 'Inoperative'; and a rated pilot or mechanic decides it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. The 91.205(c) night items are required for a night VFR flight, so they cannot be deferred for one [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]].

head: Failure
Instructor response
Source
rows: Legal for part 91 not for hire after 91.213(d), but a real hazard to weigh
Round out when the far-end runway lights appear to rise above the nose; feel for the runway with power and pitch
In a single-engine airplane at night, an alternator failure may lead to total electrical failure
Flashlight ready; the AFH blackout training practices exactly this
Best glide, turn toward an airport or away from congested areas, announce, land toward an unlighted area if the terrain is known to be suitable, landing light on in time

callout.text: Blackout landings should always be part of night pilot training as an emergency procedure [[24:228|AFH 11-11]].

body.p: Weather. Clouds and restrictions are hard to see at night, especially on dark nights or under an overcast; the first sign of trouble is usually ground lights slowly disappearing, and a halo around lights means ground fog [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]. Looking through haze to land gives much less visibility than looking straight down through it [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

bullets: Brief the temperature/dew point spread: a narrow spread may mean fog [[24:224|AFH 11-7]]. Fog seldom forms when the spread is more than 2 C [[28:222|AWH 18-2]].
Radiation fog favors clear skies and light winds, forms at night and often lasts until after sunrise [[28:222|AWH 18-2]] [[28:223|AWH 18-3]].
Wind effects are harder to detect at night, so stress forecast wind direction and speed [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].

Class G at 1,200 ft AGL or less at night: 3 SM and 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal, except 1 SM clear of clouds in a pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]] [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)(2)]].
The AFH says that even experienced pilots should fly night VFR only in unrestricted visibility, favorable winds on the surface and aloft, and no turbulence [[24:231|AFH 11-14]].
Meeting IMC at night raises risk dramatically unless pilot and airplane are IFR-equipped with an IFR plan ready to activate [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

callout.text: Coach the learner through the go/no-go. The AIH says to include the learner in risk management on dual flights, to stress assessing environmental risks such as night hazards, and to confirm the airplane's airworthiness status before the preflight [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: On a night cross-country the lights of a town ahead start to show a halo. What does it mean?
check.a: Probably ground fog; further flight in that direction calls for caution [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

chunks.title: R4 and R7: Distraction, disorientation, and currency versus proficiency

body.p: Distractions and task priority. Approach accidents become more likely when an emergency or other activity distracts from usual procedures [[24:230|AFH 11-13]]. The AIH asks instructors to teach and model the sterile flight deck: no nonessential activity during taxi, takeoff, landing and other critical phases [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

bullets: Late night, fatigue and sustained flight above 5,000 ft can make pilots less critical, less decisive and more accepting just as the hardest part of the flight arrives [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].

Instructor actions from the AIH: make individual skills well-practiced before asking for several tasks at once, teach how to handle distractions and give practice, and point out fixation and inattention when it occurs [[25:83|AIH 3-32]].
Loss of situational awareness on the surface: if conflicting information or doubt exists, do not continue the taxi or takeoff [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

Disorientation over water at night: the horizon blends with the water, and stars reflected on calm water look like a continuous field of lights [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]. A night takeoff over water can create a black-hole effect that requires an immediate shift to instruments [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

body.p: Currency versus proficiency. 61.57(b) lets a pilot carry passengers after 3 night full-stop landings in 90 days [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]]. The FAA calls these requirements minimums [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]], and says night experience is a small part of most pilots' time, so pilots should judge their own need for more proficiency before marginal night flights [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.2]].

head: Evidence
What it tells your learner
rows: Night VFR accident rate falls nearly 50 percent once a pilot reaches 100 hours, and keeps falling to 1,000
For the first 500 hours, set night personal limits higher than the rules [[25:13|AIH 1-9]]
A night ceiling under 3,000 ft or visibility under 5 miles may be unnecessary risk; the sample pilot chose 5,000 ft and 8 miles for night VFR [[30:14|RMH 2-2]]
The pilot had one hour of night time in 11 months; the NTSB named lack of recent night experience as a factor [[30:66|RMH C-3]] [[30:67|RMH C-4]]
Has its own blank for VFR night fuel reserve [[25:207|AIH D-2]]

callout.text: The PHAK's advice for coping with disorientation includes keeping night-flight currency and proficiency with both cross-country and local flights at various airfields [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]] [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Offer graduates a night refresher with a new airport, not just three laps of the home pattern.

check.q: A pilot just met 61.57(b) with three full-stop landings at the home field in calm air. Is that proficiency for a gusty night trip to an unfamiliar airport?
check.a: No. The rule is a minimum [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]]; AC 61-98E says to weigh the need for more proficiency, especially for marginal night conditions [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.2]].

chunks.title: S1: How to teach it: planning and running the first night lesson

body.p: Use the demonstration-performance method: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. The explanation is done before the flight with objectives, completion standards, a thorough briefing and the safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

head: Stage
What you do
Source
rows: Assign the learner to plan the flight: weather with the temperature/dew point spread, lighting status in the Chart Supplement and NOTAMs, black course lines. SBT is most effective when it matches the local environment

Teach K1 and K5 first (eye, dark adaptation, scanning), then lights and illusions. Brief the positive exchange of controls and what each of you does if the flight deck lights or electrical system fail
Learner leads with a white flashlight; check and tap every light, sweep the ramp
Instructor tells, instructor does: you fly it, naming each cue (edge lights, heading, positive climb on the instruments, no turn before a safe altitude)
Building blocks: straight-and-level, climbs, descents, turns and steep turns, then lights OFF segments
Learner tells, instructor does, then learner tells and does. Count the full-stop landings toward 61.109
Learner self-assessment first, then your assessment; give concrete fixes and avoid ending on a negative note

bullets: Primacy: the first night landing makes a strong impression, so make sure the learner gets it right the first time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Demonstrate exactly the way you want it practiced, including every safety step, and admit any deviation from your explanation right away [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Known to unknown: tie night landings to the day landings the learner already flies [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Guard the controls and be ready to take them; anxious learners can be very strong [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Use a visual check that the other person actually has the controls; at night that means light enough to see their hands (application).

callout.text: An unprepared learner is a serious hazard; mitigate with a syllabus, good ground instruction and a thorough brief before each flight [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]. If the learner arrives tired after a full workday, that is a no-go item, not a challenge.

check.q: In telling-and-doing, what step comes between 'instructor tells, instructor does' and 'learner tells, learner does'?
check.a: Learner tells, instructor does: the learner talks you through the maneuver while you fly [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

body.p: These are the night errors the sources name. Your job is to see them early and fix the cause, not just the symptom.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Glare and reflections on the windshield; learner cannot see outside
Dim to the minimum that still lets you read instruments and switches [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]
Airplane inches forward with power up
Hold or lock the brakes and watch for movement [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]
Heading drifts left in the dark
Inexperienced pilots relax right rudder with no visual references ahead; cue the rudder and the heading indicator [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]
Learner banks toward the pattern at a low altitude
No turns until a safe maneuvering altitude [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]
Landing light left on in haze
Glare and distortion in the climb
Turn it off once the climb is established, unless needed for collision avoidance [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]
Altimeter low for the distance; red-heavy PAPI
Cross-check altimeter and VSI against position; use the VASI [[24:227|AFH 11-10]]
Airplane floats high over the runway
Keep the descent until the landing light shows tire marks [[24:228|AFH 11-11]]
Light seems to wander; learner chases it
Scanning is the main cure for autokinesis [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]
Eyes locked on instruments or runway
Students tend to do this when concentrating on instruments or landing [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]; point it out at once [[25:83|AIH 3-32]]
Learner squints after reading a chart
Dim white light, never shone in anyone's eyes [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]]
Continuing when lost on the ground
Do not continue the taxi with any doubt; stop and ask [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]

callout.text: Errors are slips (doing something other than intended) or mistakes (doing the wrong thing as planned) [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]. A high round out from a misread cue is a mistake; fix the cue. A forgotten taxi light is a slip; fix the habit with the checklist.

check.q: Your learner rounds out too high on every night landing. What cue does the AFH give?
check.a: Continue a constant descent until the landing light reflects on the runway and tire marks are clearly visible, then round out [[24:228|AFH 11-11]].

f1.caption: Figure 11-1. Rods and cones. (AFH 11-2)
f1.alt: Cutaway of the eye. A small purple area at the back center is labeled cones for color, detail and day; a green band around the rest of the retina is labeled rods for gray, peripheral, day and night.

f2.caption: Figure 17-18. Scanning techniques. (PHAK 17-23)
f2.alt: A view over green terrain past an airplane's spinner. Numbered points 1 to 4 show a scan from far left to far right, then down and back right to left nearer the airplane, with a 10 degree overlap marked between stops.

f3.caption: FIG 2-1-5. Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI). The indication labels and color key are cropped off for the labeling game; open circles are white lights and filled circles are red. (AIM 2-1-4)
f3.alt: Five rows of four lights, each beside a runway outline. Left to right: four open circles; three open and one filled; two open and two filled; one open and three filled; four filled.

f4.caption: Figure 11-5. Establish a positive climb. (AFH 11-9)
f4.alt: A six-pack instrument panel: airspeed needle in the green arc, attitude indicator showing nose up with wings level, altimeter, turn coordinator level, heading indicator on north, and vertical speed indicator showing a climb of about 500 feet per minute.

f5.caption: Figure 11-6. Use light patterns for orientation. (AFH 11-10)
f5.alt: A night photo over a city. Two parallel lines of white runway lights run into the distance, nearly lost among streetlights and the bright green-lit streets in the foreground.

f6.caption: Figure 11-4. Position lights. (AFH 11-6)
f6.alt: Top view of an airplane at night with a red light on the left wingtip, green on the right wingtip, and white on the tail.

f7.caption: Figure 9-8. Positive exchange of flight controls. (AIH 9-9)
f7.alt: Three stacked boxes. One: the instructor says 'You have the flight controls.' Two: the learner acknowledges at once, 'I have the flight controls.' Three: the instructor again says 'You have the flight controls.'

scenario.title: A learner's first night lesson at a quiet towered field
scenario.setup: Your private learner, Dana, has 34 hours and soloed in daylight. Tonight's 1.5-hour lesson starts at 1930; evening civil twilight ends at 1915. The METAR shows clear skies, calm wind, temperature 14 C and dew point 12 C. Dana arrives straight from an office with bright lights, carrying only her phone as a flashlight. The plan is the practice area, then pattern work at a towered field with a PAPI and runway guard lights.

questions.q: Will the flight time count toward the 61.109(a)(2) night training?
questions.a: Yes; the whole flight is after 1915. Night for logging is the 14 CFR 1.1 night, after the end of evening civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]], and the training must come from an authorized instructor [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(2)]].

questions.q: What concerns you about the weather?
questions.a: A 2 C spread is close to where fog forms [[28:222|AWH 18-2]], and clear skies with light wind favor radiation fog [[28:223|AWH 18-3]], and a narrow spread may indicate fog [[24:224|AFH 11-7]]. Brief the halo-around-lights sign and a firm plan to stay near the field [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

questions.q: How do you handle Dana's eyes and her phone light?
questions.a: Brief in a dim room because adapting from bright light takes longer [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]], allow 20 to 30 minutes [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]], and lend her a dimmable white and red flashlight with spare batteries [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].

questions.q: Taxiing out, Dana sees flashing yellow lights on each side of the taxiway. What are they and what do you teach?
questions.a: Runway guard lights at a runway holding position [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10]]. Confirm the clearance to cross or hold short, and turn on all exterior lights to cross [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

questions.q: On downwind Dana spots lights ahead: green on the left, red on the right. What do you want from her?
questions.a: That airplane could be on a collision course [[24:223|AFH 11-6]]; tell you, watch whether it stays still and grows brighter [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]], and be ready to maneuver.

questions.q: How do you sequence the landings so she meets 61.109 and learns well?
questions.a: Demonstrate the first landing yourself while explaining, then have her talk you through one, then let her fly and talk [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Make each one a full stop with a flight in the pattern [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(2)(ii)]].

skills.do: The examiner will have you "Teach at least one of the elements listed in K1 through K9" (ACS AI.II.M.S1). Expect to pick or be given an element, such as night vision or traffic interpretation by position lights, and teach it as you would to a learner: objective, explanation with a visual aid, a demonstration or exercise, common errors, and a check of understanding.
skills.practice: Build a 10-minute lesson for each of K1, K2 and K9 using the demonstration-performance outline [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Use AFH Figure 11-1 for the eye [[24:219|AFH 11-2]], the PAPI drawing for lighting [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]], and AFH Figure 11-4 for position lights [[24:223|AFH 11-6]]. Teach each to another applicant and have them play a learner who stares at lights or reverses the colors.

quiz.q: Under 61.109(a)(2), the night cross-country in private pilot training must be:
options: Over 100 NM total distance
Over 100 NM straight-line distance
At least 50 NM with three landings
At least 2 hours long
quiz.why: One cross-country flight of over 100 NM total distance [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(2)(i)]].

quiz.q: Which period does the PHAK call the most dangerous for viewing?
options: Photopic
Mesopic
Scotopic
Full darkness after adaptation
quiz.why: Mesopic viewing, at dawn, dusk and full moon, is considered the most dangerous period [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]].

quiz.q: According to the AIM, how quickly can a pilot get a moderate degree of dark adaptation under dim red cockpit lighting?
options: 5 minutes
10 minutes
20 minutes
45 minutes
quiz.why: About 20 minutes; complete adaptation needs at least 30 minutes of total darkness [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]].

quiz.q: The commercial ASEL night solo or PIC requirement includes 10 takeoffs and 10 landings at:
options: Any lighted airport
An airport with an operating control tower
An airport at least 50 NM away
An airport with a PAPI
quiz.why: 5 hours in night VFR conditions with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings at an airport with an operating control tower [[60:315|14 CFR 61.129(a)(4)(ii)]].

quiz.q: About how much more sensitive to light does the AFH say the periphery of the retina, where the rods are, is than the fovea?
options: About 10 times
About 10,000 times
About 100 times
About 1,000,000 times
quiz.why: The rods are located mainly in the periphery of the retina, an area about 10,000 times more sensitive to light than the fovea; they serve night vision and show objects in shades of gray [[24:218|AFH 11-1]].

quiz.q: When may you begin a descent using a PAPI?
options: As soon as you see the lights
At 3.4 NM from the threshold
Once visually aligned with the runway
When the PAPI shows 4 white
quiz.why: Descent using the PAPI should not begin until the aircraft is visually aligned with the runway [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]].

quiz.q: Where must the white position light face?
options: Forward
Aft
Down
Toward the right wing
quiz.why: The white position light faces aft [[60:118|14 CFR 23.2530(c)]].

quiz.q: How does the AFH treat blackout landings in night training?
options: Optional for commercial students only
Prohibited without a waiver
Always included, as an emergency procedure
Only in the simulator
quiz.why: Blackout landings should always be included in night pilot training as an emergency procedure [[24:228|AFH 11-11]].

quiz.q: Under scotopic (night) vision, what visual acuity does the PHAK give?
options: 20/40, about half of normal day acuity
20/100 once the eyes are fully dark adapted
20/200 or less
20/20 if the learner uses off-center viewing
quiz.why: Under scotopic vision the cones become ineffective and visual acuity decreases to 20/200 or less: a person must stand at 20 feet to see what can normally be seen at 200 feet in daylight [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]].

quiz.q: On a night takeoff roll, what color do the runway end lights show the pilot at the far end, and what do they mean?
options: Green, marking the threshold ahead
White, the same as the runway edge lights
Red, marking the end of the runway
Yellow, for the last 2,000 ft
quiz.why: The lights marking the ends of the runway emit red toward the runway to show the end of the runway to a departing aircraft, and green outward from the runway end to show the threshold to landing aircraft [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]]. Yellow is the caution zone color of the edge lights on the last part of an instrument runway [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your student has 85-day-old night training at her home airport and an A.5 endorsement from you. She wants a night solo there in 10 days. What applies?
options: She may go; the endorsement has no expiration
She may go if her day solo endorsement is current, since it covers night flights too
New night training and endorsement first; the training will be over 90 days old
She needs a night cross-country first
final_quiz.why: The night solo endorsement must come from an instructor who gave the training within the 90 days before the flight [[60:277|14 CFR 61.87(o)(3)]]; A.5 expires 90 calendar days from the night training [[12:41|AC 61-65K A.5]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot trained in and living in Alaska got a private certificate without night training 13 calendar months ago and never did it. What is his status?
options: Fine, but no night flying
His certificate is invalid for use until he does the night training
He must retake the practical test
He may fly at night with an instructor's endorsement only, until the training is done
final_quiz.why: Without the night training within 12 calendar months, the certificate becomes invalid for use until he complies [[60:307|14 CFR 61.110(b)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: In the night briefing your learner mentions she flies in monovision contact lenses, one for distance and one for near. What does the AFH say?
options: Fine at night, because one eye then handles the instruments while the other one watches outside
They suppress one eye at a time and impair depth perception; the FAA recommends against them
They are a problem only by day, since the rods ignore the lens power at night
They help in the dark, since the near lens sharpens the dim instrument panel
final_quiz.why: Monovision lenses make the pilot use one eye at a time, suppressing the other, which impairs binocular vision and depth perception; the FAA recommends not using them when piloting an aircraft [[24:221|AFH 11-4]].

final_quiz.q: You and a learner spent 30 minutes at 12,000 ft without oxygen and descended to 8,000 ft. Her night vision is still dim and washed out. What does the PHAK say?
options: It returns as soon as you descend
Visual acuity may not return for over an hour
It returns within 10 minutes on red light
Only supplemental oxygen at 8,000 ft restores it
final_quiz.why: After a climb from 8,000 to 12,000 ft for 30 minutes, a descent may not restore acuity for over an hour [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]].

final_quiz.q: Descending at night toward a busy airport, your learner turns the landing light off to save the bulb. What does the AIM encourage?
options: Landing lights off below 10,000 ft at night, so other pilots' night vision is not spoiled near airports
Landing lights on below 10,000 ft, day or night, especially within 10 miles of an airport
Landing lights on only inside Class B, C and D airspace, where the traffic is heaviest
Landing lights on only on final, since that is the one place other pilots look for them
final_quiz.why: Pilots are encouraged to turn on their landing lights when operating below 10,000 ft, day or night, especially within 10 miles of any airport, but not all aircraft have them and some pilots may not turn them on [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

final_quiz.q: A rental Cessna has an inoperative landing light, no MEL, and is flown for training, not for hire. The light is deactivated and placarded, and you judge it no hazard. Which is true?
options: The flight is illegal at night
It is legal under 91.213(d), but it remains a hazard to weigh
It needs a special flight permit to fly at night without the light
It is legal only with a flight review endorsement
final_quiz.why: The landing light is required only when operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]], so 91.213(d) can apply [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]; the RMH still calls it a hazard for night operation [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

final_quiz.q: Ahead and to your right, at your altitude, you see only a red light. It does not move across the windshield and is getting brighter. What do you teach?
options: It is moving away; ignore it
It is overtaking you from behind
Collision course; the airplane on your right has the right-of-way, so you give way
It is a lighted tower, since lights that do not move are fixed; check the chart for it
final_quiz.why: No relative motion and growing larger means take evasive action [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]; the airplane on the right has the right-of-way when converging [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]].

final_quiz.q: Before a night takeoff, your learner leaves the panel and dome lights at full brightness, and the windshield shows reflections. What does the AFH say?
options: Keep them bright so she can read the instruments easily during the climb
Dim the flight deck lights to the minimum that lets her read instruments and switches
Turn them all off and use only a flashlight until reaching cruise altitude
Switch to the red dome light only, since red light removes windshield reflections at any brightness
final_quiz.why: Adjust the flight deck lights to a minimum brightness that still allows reading the instruments and switches but does not hinder outside vision; dimming them also eliminates reflections on the windshield and windows [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing out at night over a dark lake, the learner says the horizon is 'that line of lights' and banks to level with it. What first?
options: Tell him to keep the wings level with the shoreline lights, which mark the horizon
Attitude indicator first; shoreline lights can make a false horizon
Turn on the landing light
Descend to see the water
final_quiz.why: Shoreline lights can be mistaken for stars and create a false horizon [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]; over water the horizon blends with the water [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]; use the instruments [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

final_quiz.q: A strobe reflecting off the wing is making your learner queasy and dizzy. What do the sources suggest?
options: Increase cockpit lighting to drown it out
Eliminate or screen out the flickering light source
Stare at the light until you adapt
Descend below the cloud base
final_quiz.why: Pilots should eliminate or screen out any light causing a reaction to flicker [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]; proper scanning helps prevent flicker vertigo [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]].

final_quiz.q: Three graduates ask for night refreshers. Which plan best matches the PHAK and AC 61-98E?
options: Three full-stop landings at the home field, since 61.57(b) currency is the FAA's standard
Night cross-country and local work at several airfields, more before marginal trips
A ground lesson only
A simulator session with no landings
final_quiz.why: The PHAK says keep night currency and proficiency with cross-country and local operations at various airfields [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]; AC 61-98E treats 61.57 as a minimum [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]].

final_quiz.q: Cruising at 6,500 ft at night, your learner cannot pick the destination's runway lights out of a bright town glow. What does the AFH say about altitude and lights?
options: Higher is better: the higher you are, the more of the separate light groups you can pick out
From about 2,000 ft lights show one by one; from 5,000 ft up they may merge into one mass
Lights look the same from any altitude, so only the beacon can find the airport
Lights merge only below 1,000 ft AGL, so stay high until the runway is in sight
final_quiz.why: At an altitude of 2,000 ft a group of lights on an object may be seen individually, while at 5,000 ft or higher the same lights could appear to be one solid light mass [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]. Fly toward the rotating beacon until the runway lights can be told apart [[24:227|AFH 11-10]].

final_quiz.q: A newly certificated private pilot with 80 hours says 61.57 night currency is all she needs for night trips. What does the AIH's accident data suggest?
options: Night accident rates are flat after the checkride, so currency is the right standard
The night VFR accident rate drops nearly 50 percent by 100 hours; set higher limits early
Night risk falls only after 1,000 hours, so she should not fly at night at all before then
The night accident rate rises with experience, as pilots grow overconfident
final_quiz.why: The night VFR accident rate decreases by nearly 50 percent once a pilot obtains 100 hours and keeps decreasing to the 1,000-hour level, so for the first 500 hours pilots flying VFR at night might want higher personal limits than the regulations require [[25:13|AIH 1-9]].

takeaways: Private night training: 3 hours, a cross-country over 100 NM total distance, and 10 full-stop landings in the pattern.
Student night solo needs your night training at that airport and a make and model endorsement within 90 days.
Night vision is rod vision: scan, look off center, and protect dark adaptation from bright light.
Dim red for the outside view, dim white for charts, and never a flashlight in anyone's eyes.
Use the instruments to confirm a positive climb and use the PAPI or VASI and the altimeter on every approach.
Read traffic by its lights: a red and green pair with red on the right is coming toward you, white alone is a tail, brighter and still is a collision course.
Currency is the legal floor; teach learners to set night personal minimums well above it.
cfi_notes: Sources disagree on altitude: PHAK says night vision declines measurably above 4,000 ft pressure altitude [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]]; the AFH says hypoxia that impairs vision can start above 5,000 ft at night without oxygen [[24:221|AFH 11-4]], and the AIM says cabin pressure altitudes above 5,000 ft impair dark adaptation [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]]. Teach that degradation starts low and oxygen helps; the PHAK suggests considering oxygen where not required at night [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]].
Flicker vertigo frequency: the AFH gives 1 to 20 hertz [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]; the PHAK says 4 to 20 cycles per second [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]. The cure is the same.

Off-center viewing: PHAK 17-22 says 5 to 10 degrees off center [[1:444|PHAK 17-22]], while PHAK 17-23 and AC 90-48E say about 10 degrees [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]] [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]]. Teach 10 degrees.

Scanning rules differ by lighting: the AIM's general traffic-scan technique uses eye movements of no more than 10 degrees and at least 1 second per area [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6]]; the PHAK night technique uses stops about 30 degrees wide of no more than 2 to 3 seconds [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]]. Do not mix them up when you brief.

The AFH chapter opens by saying night flying should not be encouraged except for certificated pilots with night knowledge and experience [[24:218|AFH 11-1]], yet 61.109 requires night training for students. Read it as: night is for trained pilots, and your training is how they become trained.
Who is PIC on a night dual lesson, and so whether you must meet 61.57(b) yourself, is not addressed in the sources read for this lesson; stay night current so the question never matters.

The no-landing-light round out cue (far-end runway lights rising above the nose) requires a very timely round out [[24:228|AFH 11-11]]; demonstrate it yourself first and only on a long, well-lit runway (application).
AC 91-73B is voluntary guidance; its lighting and line-up advice is not a rule [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7h(1)]].
Teach risk management on night cross-countries as a full analysis the learner prepares and you approve [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].
gaps: The sources give no lighting field-of-coverage angles for position lights; 14 CFR 23.2530 states only colors and placement [[60:118|14 CFR 23.2530(c)]]. Do not teach exact angles from memory.
Electrical load figures for landing and taxi lights, and any light duty limits, are in the POH/AFM.
The sources do not give a step-by-step night syllabus or how many night lessons a typical learner needs; build it from your school's syllabus and the learner's progress.
Sunset, civil twilight and the 1-hour-after-sunset times come from an almanac or FAA tool for the date and place; the sources give only the definitions [[24:218|AFH 11-1]].
Specific pilot-controlled lighting frequencies and any non-standard systems are only in the Chart Supplement [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

activities.title: True or false: guarding your learner's night vision
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Red cockpit light can make it hard to focus on objects inside the airplane.
cards.why: True. The AIM says red light distorts chart colors and can cause serious difficulty focusing inside [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]].

cards.s: Eating extra vitamin A improves night vision beyond normal.
cards.why: False. A lack of vitamin A impairs night vision, but high quantities do not improve it [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]].

cards.s: Adapting to the dark takes longer coming from a bright room than from a dim room.
Once at cruise altitude, night vision is already as good as it will get.
cards.why: False. Allow time after reaching altitude; night vision keeps improving until optimum adaptation [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]].

cards.s: The night blind spot can hide a larger object as the distance to it grows.
Under red light, cyan chart symbols appear black.
cards.why: True. Magenta and yellow look red and cyan looks black [[24:221|AFH 11-4]].

activities.title: Night numbers you will brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Sunset is 1812 local. At what time (hhmm) does the 61.57(b) period for night passenger currency begin?
A learner has logged 2.2 hours of night training, including the long cross-country. How many more hours of night training does 61.109(a)(2) require?
The same learner has 6 night full-stop landings in the pattern. How many more does she need?
Your airplane burns 8.4 gallons per hour at normal cruise. How many gallons is the night VFR reserve beyond the first point of intended landing?
Using the PHAK night scan (stops about 30 degrees wide, each overlapping the last by 10 degrees), how many stops does it take to cover 120 degrees of windshield?
items.why: First stop covers 30 degrees; each later stop adds 30 - 10 = 20. 30 + 20 x 4 = 110 is short; 30 + 20 x 5 = 130 covers it, so 6 stops [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].

activities.title: A night dual cross-country, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying a learner's 61.109 night cross-country, 110 NM total over mostly dark farmland with a lake near the destination.

steps.s: 1800 briefing: destination clear, calm wind, temperature 9 C, dew point 7 C, and both are forecast to meet by 2300. You plan to land back at 2200.
options: Go as planned; you will be back before the forecast fog
Go, but brief fog signs and a firm turnaround time and alternate, and check updates en route
Cancel; any fog forecast is a no-go
Go and plan to climb above any fog
steps.why: A narrow spread may mean fog [[24:224|AFH 11-7]], and radiation fog favors clear skies and light winds [[28:223|AWH 18-3]]. The AIH's model is a learner who checks weather hourly and plans to divert at the first sign [[25:83|AIH 3-32]].

steps.s: Taxi: the learner hesitates at an unlit intersection and says the sign does not match the diagram.
options: Keep rolling slowly while you look
Stop off the runway, sort it out with the diagram and ask ground for progressive taxi
Turn on the strobes to see better
Take the controls and keep going
steps.why: With any doubt, do not continue the taxi [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]; stop and ask for progressive taxi [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]].

steps.s: Takeoff: at 300 ft AGL the learner starts a turn toward the course over a dark area.
options: Allow it; the course is that way
Have her level the wings and climb on the instruments to a safe maneuvering altitude first
Turn on the landing light to see the ground
Reduce power
steps.why: No turns until a safe maneuvering altitude, with a positive climb on the attitude indicator, VSI and altimeter [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

steps.s: Cruise: the town lights ahead slowly grow a halo.
options: Continue and descend to stay below it
Treat it as ground fog: turn back or divert while the alternate is clear
Climb higher to see over it
Turn up the panel lights
steps.why: A halo around ground lights indicates ground fog, and further flight that way calls for caution [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]; the PHAK says decide early to turn and land at an alternate [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]].

steps.s: At the alternate, final over a dark lake: the PAPI shows 1 white and 3 red, and the learner says the runway looks fine.
options: Continue; the runway looks fine
Correct up to 2 white and 2 red and cross-check the altimeter; go around if position is in doubt
Dive to the runway
Ignore the PAPI over water
steps.why: 1 white and 3 red is slightly low [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]]; a black-hole approach can end short, so use the VASI or PAPI and go around when in doubt [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].
